events.title: ECMAScript 2022 standardized
events.summary: Ecma adopted ECMAScript 2022 in June 2022 — adding class fields, top-level `await`, `Array.at()`, and `Object.hasOwn()`.
events.about: ES2022 let modules use top-level await for cleaner async bootstrapping, and class fields removed constructor boilerplate for React/Vue class components and Node services. `at(-1)` finally gave arrays a readable 'last element' accessor.

narrative.whyChosen: ES2022 delivered top-level await and class fields that frameworks and bundlers had polyfilled for years.
narrative.whyImportant: Module-level async initialization became standard without IIFE wrappers.
narrative.problemSolved: Developers needed awkward patterns to await data before exporting module bindings.

events.title: Internet Explorer 11 retired
events.summary: Microsoft retired the Internet Explorer 11 desktop app on June 15, 2022 — ending 27 years of the browser that once held over 90% market share.
events.about: Opening IE on Windows 10 redirected users to Microsoft Edge; IE mode in Edge kept legacy intranet apps running. The retirement applied to the IE11 desktop app on consumer Windows 10 — Windows 10 LTSC, Windows Server, and Windows 7 ESU editions retained IE11 support. For developers, it was the final break from ActiveX-only sites, `-ms-` hacks, and the IE6–IE11 compatibility matrix.

narrative.whyChosen: IE's retirement closed the longest chapter in browser history and the era of building for one dominant engine.
narrative.whyImportant: It forced the last holdouts off a browser with no security updates and shrinking web compatibility.
narrative.problemSolved: Microsoft could not maintain a separate legacy browser alongside Chromium-based Edge indefinitely.

events.title: HTTP/3 standardized
events.summary: RFC 9114 published HTTP/3 on June 6, 2022 — HTTP semantics mapped onto the QUIC transport protocol over UDP.
events.about: HTTP/3 keeps HTTP methods and status codes but replaces TCP with QUIC — faster handshakes, per-stream flow control, and no TCP head-of-line blocking. QPACK compresses headers like HPACK did for HTTP/2. Major browsers and CDNs enabled HTTP/3 by default for lower latency on lossy networks.

narrative.whyChosen: HTTP/3 completed the HTTP performance story started by HTTP/2 and Google's QUIC experiments.
narrative.whyImportant: It is now the preferred transport for many sites, especially on mobile and high-latency links.
narrative.problemSolved: TCP's head-of-line blocking still hurt HTTP/2 on unreliable networks; QUIC fixes that at the transport layer.
